107.fortune: Not every relationship we become attached to is with a person. Sometimes you think something is your only refuge while it brings you closer to danger every day. If leaving it seems impossible, maybe it's time to name that dependence honestly. Loyalty to something that destroys you isn't love.
107.history: The title deliberately leads the listener to imagine a romance, but the 'girlfriend' in Tupac's story is a metaphor for a gun. Through the image of romantic loyalty, he links violence with dependence on a weapon. Released on the 1996 Makaveli album, the track should not be read simply as a love song.

108.headline: Freedom matters more than money
108.fortune: Your bank account may have grown without making you feel any freer. If you've sacrificed sleep, peace, and important people in your life to achieve something, perhaps it's time to redefine success. Today, hold on to one thing money can't buy. Freedom means more than an open door.
108.history: On this track, Tupac pays tribute to prisoners, including political prisoners, and speaks about anxiety, fame, and the value of freedom. In the lyrics, money means less when measured against freedom. It belongs to the last album recorded during his lifetime, released after his death in November 1996.

109.headline: Speak bravely, but make sure you speak accurately.
109.fortune: When you see conspiracy everywhere, even the truth starts to look hostile. Perhaps betrayal still makes you angry and you want to name every guilty party. Before turning suspicion into an accusation, recognize the distance between evidence and interpretation. Speaking up takes courage; speaking carefully takes even more.
109.history: On the closing Makaveli track, Tupac verbally attacks several music-industry figures and former associates and makes claims about betrayal and the 1994 shooting. Those allegations represent his perspective, not established facts. The song was recorded in 1996 and released after his death.
109.details: 2Pac | Recorded summer 1996 | Released November 5, 1996, posthumously | Makaveli

110.headline: Sometimes a voice grows louder after its owner is gone.
110.fortune: Sometimes someone's voice becomes louder only after they are gone. Maybe unfinished words from your past keep returning to your mind. Not every memory will give you a clear answer. What matters is finding your own meaning without inventing a story that never happened. Some beginnings grow out of an absence.
110.history: A short edited introduction to R U Still Down?, this piece relies more on repeated audio samples and Tupac phrases than on a newly composed full song. The album appeared posthumously in November 1997, so 'Redemption' should not be treated as a story newly written by Tupac at that time.
110.details: 2Pac | Older recordings edited later | Released November 1997, posthumously | R U Still Down?, disc one

111.headline: The thrill of escape is not the same as freedom.
111.fortune: When every day feels like a chase, peace may elude you even in sleep. Maybe you have chosen a path that constantly forces you to lie or run to preserve it. Before the next step, consider the toll on you and those close to you. The thrill of getting away is not real freedom.
111.history: The song tells a harsh story involving drug dealing, police pursuit, and exchanges of gunfire. Tupac refers to fear of arrest and the strain on his mother. The 1997 R U Still Down? release draws on older recordings, largely from 1992-1994. It is not a verified account of one particular chase.
111.details: 2Pac | Recorded mainly 1992-1994; edited later | Released November 1997, posthumously | R U Still Down?, disc one

112.headline: Success can bring an old question back: who's still there?
112.fortune: When you become successful, an old question returns: who is still the same person? Maybe you resent how others have changed, but you have changed too. Instead of putting everyone through endless loyalty tests, look at their actions. Do not confuse devotion with remaining frozen in the past. People can grow and still care about you.
112.history: On the title track, Tupac addresses loyalty, fame, shifting relationships, and his street roots. Selected from recordings made before his death, it was released on the posthumous 1997 album. The question in the title points to the bond between artist and audience and the endurance of loyalty.
112.details: 2Pac | Recorded mainly 1992-1994; edited later | Released November 1997, posthumously | R U Still Down?, disc one

113.headline: Understanding someone's anger does not mean accepting their violence.
113.fortune: Some people learn to fight before they ever get a chance to feel safe. You may see someone's rage and assume that is all they are. Try to understand where the pain came from, but do not let it hurt you. Learning why someone became violent does not mean you have to accept their violence.
113.history: In 'Hellrazor,' Tupac addresses poverty, young lives lost, police behavior, racism, and the anger of a generation that feels rejected. The title evokes a fiery rebel. Released in November 1997, it comes from earlier sessions and should not be mistaken for a reflection of Tupac's life in the release year.
113.details: 2Pac | Recorded mainly 1992-1994; edited later | Released November 1997, posthumously | R U Still Down?, disc one

114.headline: A tough image should not become a prison.
114.fortune: Sometimes you feel more afraid than ever while trying to look fearless. When all your energy goes into displaying strength, you may forget what actually deserves protection. You do not have to be ready for conflict at every moment to keep your respect. The image you built should serve your life, not imprison it.
114.history: Tupac constructs a boastful, hard-edged street-rapper persona, discussing money, danger, and readiness for confrontation. Released in the 1997 collection R U Still Down?, the original performance dates to an earlier phase of his career. Its tone is aggressive and theatrical.
114.details: 2Pac | Recorded mainly 1992-1994; edited later | Released November 1997, posthumously | R U Still Down?, disc one

115.headline: Sometimes the better question is: where do we go now?
115.fortune: Sometimes the best question is not who was to blame, but where to go from here. If you have felt stuck for a long time, perhaps you have spent so much energy replaying the past that no room remains for your next choice. Not every answer appears immediately, but you can change the questions. You need not pretend to have a map.
115.history: Although issued as an interlude, this track contains an extended Tupac spoken passage on violence against children, poverty, unemployment, and police pressure. He also refers to 1994 and friends who died. Released posthumously in 1997, it retains the protest spirit of his earlier recordings.
115.details: 2Pac | Recorded mainly 1992-1994; edited later | Released November 1997, posthumously | R U Still Down?, disc one

116.headline: If justice is missing here, should we only hope for it elsewhere?
116.fortune: If the world seems to have no room for some people, is justice waiting for them somewhere else? Maybe you are tired of watching suffering that nobody seems responsible for. Hope matters, but it must not become an excuse to ignore today's pain. An imagined heaven should not stop us from making this world fairer.
116.history: Tupac asks whether heaven, too, has a neighborhood for the poor and excluded, addressing poverty, racism, violence, and inequality. A version was released as part of the 1997 collection and as a single. Its political themes reach back to his earlier career, and his vocal recording predates his death.
116.details: 2Pac | Recorded mainly 1992-1994; edited later | Released November 1997, posthumously | R U Still Down?, disc one

117.headline: Despair is a terrible accountant of your future.
117.fortune: The most dangerous moment can be when you believe you have nothing left to lose. Maybe you are exhausted and one sudden decision feels capable of ending the uncertainty. Yet even under pressure, things may matter deeply to your future self. Do not make one difficult night the verdict on your entire life. Despair is a poor judge of tomorrow.
117.history: Tupac describes poverty, distrust, confrontation, and the feeling of reaching the end of the road. The title reflects someone who thinks risk carries little cost. Released on R U Still Down? in 1997, the vocals came from several years earlier.
117.details: 2Pac | Recorded mainly 1992-1994; edited later | Released November 1997, posthumously | R U Still Down?, disc one

118.headline: Money opens doors, but it cannot heal everything.
118.fortune: Money can open new doors, but it cannot close every old wound. Maybe your income has finally improved and you feel compelled to show your success to everybody. Before spending to prove yourself, ask what actually brings stability to your life. Having money is one thing; knowing how to live with it is another.
118.history: Centered on earning money, ambition, and the economics of street life, the song depicts a character trying to rise above scarcity through a path full of risk and displays of power. It was released on the 1997 posthumous album R U Still Down? from earlier recordings.
118.details: 2Pac | Recorded mainly 1992-1994; edited later | Released November 1997, posthumously | R U Still Down?, disc one

119.headline: You don't need an exaggerated story to belong.
119.fortune: You do not have to make your life story bigger than it is to be accepted. Maybe your social circle is full of people making grand claims, and silence feels like losing. But an identity built on lies costs effort to maintain every day. A real person may attract less attention, yet never has to keep acting out yesterday's invented role.
119.history: Tupac and Richie Rich mock false claims about street credibility and friendship. The track nevertheless includes misogynistic insults and a reference to Mike Tyson. Drawn from older recordings, it appeared on the posthumous R U Still Down? collection in 1997.
119.details: 2Pac | Recorded mainly 1992-1994; edited later | Released November 1997, posthumously | R U Still Down?, disc one

120.headline: A wall that blocks enemies can also block friends.
120.fortune: When a few people disappoint you, the temptation is to shut everyone out. Maybe you want to declare nobody deserves trust. Do not deny your anger, but do not let a handful of relationships become the rule for all humanity. Leaving someone harmful is your right; isolating yourself can become a new punishment. High walls keep friends out too.
120.history: Tupac directs his anger and distrust at people he regards as opportunists or betrayers. The lyrics are deliberately harsh and dismissive, dramatizing alienation. This version appeared on the posthumous album R U Still Down? in November 1997; its exact recording date is uncertain.
120.details: 2Pac | Recorded mainly 1992-1994; edited later | Released November 1997, posthumously | R U Still Down?, disc one

121.headline: Not every shout is a sign of strength.
121.fortune: Maybe you have spent so long trying not to be underestimated that you are always ready to answer back. That turns every gathering into a competition you never wanted. Before reacting, ask what actually deserves your energy and reputation. You do not have to answer every provocation to prove that you can.
121.history: An aggressive, energetic track from Tupac's older recordings, issued posthumously on R U Still Down? in 1997. He emphasizes street credibility, retaliation, and displays of power, even mentioning his 2Pacalypse era. Despite its title, the song is not a gentle warning against guns; its dominant tone is confrontational.
121.details: 2Pac | R U Still Down? (Remember Me) | Released November 17, 1997, posthumously; recording date uncertain

122.headline: Sometimes the tough persona becomes bigger than the person.
122.fortune: You might believe that showing a moment of vulnerability would cost you everything. But a life spent defending an image leaves little room to rest. Ask which decisions came from genuine need and which came from a need to display power. Playing a role has a price, too.
122.history: Tupac sets out a harsh street-based image of a 'gangster' through money, weapons, sex, and survival. Some lyrics are explicitly misogynistic and violent. The song was released on disc one of R U Still Down? in 1997, but Tupac's vocal was recorded before his death.
122.details: 2Pac | R U Still Down? (Remember Me) | Released November 17, 1997, posthumously; recording date uncertain

123.headline: Being prepared is not the same as expecting disaster.
123.fortune: When you have stopped trusting everyone, even silence can sound threatening. Caution sometimes saves you, but if your whole life turns into guarding yourself, good things pass you by as well. Ask where danger truly exists and where an old fear is speaking. You cannot wear armor forever.
123.history: Opening disc two of R U Still Down?, Tupac describes police pressure, street rivalry, and readiness to retaliate. The lyrics are threatening and deeply distrustful. The track was issued in 1997, but reliable public sources do not establish its exact original recording date.
123.details: 2Pac | R U Still Down? (Remember Me) | Released November 17, 1997, posthumously; recording date uncertain

124.headline: Freedom begins with knowing what comes next.
124.fortune: You may have spent a long time waiting for a difficult chapter to end, saving every dream for the day the door finally opens. But release is not a plan for living. Think not only about escaping a restriction, but about the choice that follows. An open door is an opportunity; you still choose the road.
124.history: The song is structured as a dramatic prison narrative involving contact with the outside world and hopes of release, mixed with harsh threats toward enemies. Tupac refuses to treat imprisonment as the end of his story. This version appeared on disc two of R U Still Down? in 1997 and is distinct from 'When I Get Free II.'
124.details: 2Pac | R U Still Down? (Remember Me) | Released November 17, 1997, posthumously; recording date uncertain

125.headline: Sometimes staying alive is its own quiet victory.
125.fortune: Perhaps these days all you can manage are the necessities, and it feels as though you are getting nowhere. You do not have to turn every hardship into a beautiful lesson. Some days simply need to be survived. Give yourself room to endure. Strength does not always make a sound.
125.history: Among the more compassionate songs on R U Still Down?, Tupac addresses childhood poverty, hardship on the streets, and people he has lost, urging listeners to keep going. Its gentler outlook contrasts with the same album's threatening tracks. Recorded in his lifetime, it was released after his death in 1997.
125.details: 2Pac | R U Still Down? (Remember Me) | Released November 17, 1997, posthumously

126.headline: When you feel out of control, pretending will not help.
126.fortune: Long-term pressure can turn even simple decisions into battles. You may need a pause and someone safe to talk to more than another round of advice. Notice the anger without allowing it to do your thinking for you. Take the pressure seriously before it becomes the shape of your life.
126.history: With Big Syke and Spice 1, Tupac explores psychological pressure, distrust, violence, and a feeling of coming apart. The title expresses a loss of control, not a basis for diagnosing Tupac medically. Released posthumously on R U Still Down?, the track's exact recording date is uncertain.
126.details: 2Pac | R U Still Down? (Remember Me) | Released November 17, 1997, posthumously; recording date uncertain

127.headline: One betrayal is not a verdict on everyone.
127.fortune: When somebody lets you down, it can be tempting to put everyone in the same category. Do not let one painful experience poison every future relationship. You can maintain boundaries while giving people the chance to show who they are. Your anger may be understandable, but generalizing it is not necessarily fair.
127.history: Tupac criticizes superficial relationships, opportunism, and distrust. The song also contains real gender-based insults and sweeping generalizations. This fortune does not endorse those attitudes; it reflects on their consequences. The track appeared on disc two of the posthumous 1997 album R U Still Down?.
127.details: 2Pac | R U Still Down? (Remember Me) | Released November 17, 1997, posthumously

128.headline: Love shouldn't make you lose yourself
128.fortune: Love becomes dangerous when you forget yourself to keep it. Maybe you've repeatedly done things that went against your judgment and peace of mind simply because you didn't want to lose someone. Having feelings isn't wrong, but losing every boundary can hurt you. Look at the relationship from the outside for a moment. Loving someone shouldn't mean disappearing.
128.history: Featuring Eric Williams of Blackstreet in its released version, this song addresses emotional attraction, betrayal, dependence, and decisions made for love. It samples Bobby Caldwell's 'What You Won't Do for Love.' The familiar version appeared after Tupac's death on the 1997 album and became a successful single.

129.headline: Disagreement is not always an act of war.
129.fortune: After living on the defensive for too long, even an ordinary criticism can feel like an attack. Perhaps you need to distinguish competition, disrespect, and real danger all over again. Some relationships improve with distance; others improve through talking. Before calling someone an enemy, make sure you are seeing them clearly.
129.history: In this collaboration with Dramacydal, Tupac warns others not to make enemies of him. The lyrics rely on street reputation, threats, and violent responses, not calm dialogue. Released posthumously on R U Still Down?, it also reflects his earlier work with rappers who later formed part of Outlawz.
129.details: 2Pac | R U Still Down? (Remember Me) | Released November 17, 1997, posthumously

130.headline: Not everything left behind is a wound.
130.fortune: Maybe you left a neighborhood, home, or people because life there was difficult, yet you still love small moments from that time. Growing up does not require denying every root. You can acknowledge the painful truths and remember the kindness too. Returning to a memory is not always taking a step backward.
130.history: Tupac remembers Oakland and the people around him: parties, children, elders, and those who helped him through poverty. He moves from dreams of dealing drugs to being encouraged to rap, balancing hardship with affection. This older recording was released on R U Still Down? in 1997.
130.details: 2Pac | R U Still Down? (Remember Me) | Released November 17, 1997, posthumously

131.headline: One terrible mistake should not define a teenager's whole life.
131.fortune: Maybe you know someone who was drawn into the adult world far too young. Judging is easy; understanding the path that brought them there is harder. Responsibility does not disappear, but the possibility of a second chance still matters. Justice must ask both 'What did you do?' and 'How did you get here?'
131.history: Tupac speaks through a fictional sixteen-year-old awaiting execution, addressing his mother about injustice, fear, and lost opportunities. It is an artistic narrative about the criminal justice system, not a record of Tupac's own sentencing. The track was released on R U Still Down? in 1997.
131.details: 2Pac | R U Still Down? (Remember Me) | Released November 17, 1997, posthumously

132.headline: A good comeback should not repeat the old mistakes.
132.fortune: After leaving a difficult period behind, you may feel desperate to make up for lost time. You want everyone to know they cannot limit you anymore. But rushing to show power can carry you straight back into the trouble you escaped. Freedom includes the ability to choose a different response.
132.history: Separate from 'When I Get Free,' this track has a dialogue-based opening and a narrative about getting out of prison. Threats and a hunger for money after release shape its tone, rather than peaceful reflection. Both songs appeared on disc two of the 1997 collection; the exact original recording date is unknown.
132.details: 2Pac | R U Still Down? (Remember Me) | Released November 17, 1997, posthumously; recording date uncertain

133.headline: Nobody writes the story of your success alone.
133.fortune: While trying to prove yourself, you may slowly forget the people who stood beside you. Friends from the beginning and companions through hard days have all left their mark. Instead of thinking about your opponents, remember who helped you get here. Gratitude is part of having a memory.
133.history: This short interlude is a montage of Tupac's spoken remarks about his early career, underground music, and collaborators. Despite its poetic title, it is not a complete narrative song. Released on disc two of R U Still Down? in 1997, it offers a glimpse of his beginnings.
133.details: 2Pac | R U Still Down? (Remember Me) | Interlude released November 17, 1997, posthumously

134.headline: Sometimes the fear of dying steals the life you still have.
134.fortune: The hardest fear is not always death itself; sometimes it is spending every day in dread. Maybe anxiety follows you even when no immediate danger is present. Fear can take away the very life you are trying to protect. You need not answer every enormous question today. Living is more than counting possible disasters.
134.history: In one of this collection's darkest tracks, Tupac addresses death, guilt, suspicion, loneliness, and prayer. The narrator repeatedly wonders whom he can trust. Its bleak mood should not be interpreted as a literal prediction of Tupac's death. The recording was released posthumously in 1997.
134.details: 2Pac | R U Still Down? (Remember Me) | Released November 17, 1997, posthumously

135.headline: Real friendship is not measured in group photos.
135.fortune: When everyone surrounds you, it can be hard to tell who will stay. The answer gets clearer when nobody feels like listening to your troubles. Perhaps it is time to measure your relationships by their depth rather than their number. A friend who answers in the hard moments is worth the effort.
135.history: Released on the Gridlock'd soundtrack in January 1997, for a film in which Tupac starred. Made with producer Johnny 'J,' the song reflects on loyalty and friendship amid incarceration, danger, and distrust. Tupac recorded it before his death; contemporary reporting described it as an All Eyez on Me outtake.
135.details: 2Pac | Gridlock'd: The Soundtrack | Released January 28, 1997, posthumously; recorded before September 1996

136.headline: Sometimes everyone is moving and nobody gets anywhere.
136.fortune: Your days may be full of travel, rushing, and unfinished tasks, yet you still feel stuck. Activity is not always progress. You need not escape the traffic immediately, but you can start recognizing routes that leave you exhausted without bringing you closer. Sometimes the useful question is simply, 'Why am I stuck here?'
136.history: Released on the 1997 Gridlock'd soundtrack, this song combines the Eight Mile Road performance with Tupac's contribution. Traffic becomes an image of a life trapped by poverty, work, violence, and social dead ends. Its release after his death does not mean the recording was made in 1997.
136.details: 2Pac | Gridlock'd: The Soundtrack | Released January 28, 1997, posthumously; recorded earlier

137.headline: Surviving is important; living well matters too.
137.fortune: When life gets hard, it is easy to mistake enduring pain for toughness. Maybe you have not allowed yourself to feel weak for years. But fighting without a break does not necessarily make you safer. Look from a little distance: which pressures are truly beyond your control, and which are made worse by your choices?
137.history: Produced in a version by Daz Dillinger, this track was issued on the Gang Related soundtrack in October 1997; Tupac also starred in the film. It reflects economic hardship, prison, suspicion, and dangerous choices in street life. Its aggressive delivery sits beside the claim that life itself is hard.
137.details: 2Pac | Gang Related: The Soundtrack | Released October 7, 1997, posthumously; recorded earlier

138.headline: Look in the rearview mirror; don't live in it
138.fortune: Don't always look in the rearview mirror, but don't forget it either. Maybe something from the past still follows you: a mistake, a relationship, or a missed opportunity. Looking back is useful for understanding, rather than living in the same scene. Learn from what you've been through, then look ahead again. Driving with your eyes fixed behind you isn't the way out.
138.history: This collaboration between Tupac and the Outlawz appeared on the soundtrack of Gang Related in 1997. Its theme is looking back while danger and pursuit continue, and the rearview mirror metaphor fits the film's atmosphere. The recording dates from Tupac's lifetime, although the final release came after his death.

139.headline: Before joining a group, consider the cost of belonging.
139.fortune: You may be copying behavior that does not feel like yours just to be accepted. Loyalty matters, but if people demand that you hurt others to prove it, the definition needs to change. Being part of a group should not mean switching off your own judgment.
139.history: With Outlawz, Tupac emphasizes group identity, militant loyalty, and confrontation with rivals. The track belongs to his Death Row era and was released after his death on the October 1997 Gang Related soundtrack. The fortune's focus on the price of belonging is an independent interpretation of its confrontational language.
139.details: 2Pac feat. Outlawz | Gang Related: The Soundtrack | Released October 7, 1997, posthumously

140.headline: Not every busy road leads you home.
140.fortune: Being lost does not always mean you cannot see the path. Sometimes you know where you are going and fear arriving there. Maybe money, loyalty, and peace of mind are pulling you in different directions. A choice can look profitable while leaving you empty inside. Before moving again, ask what part of yourself you would leave behind.
140.history: Featuring Outlawz, this song appeared on the 1997 Gang Related soundtrack for a film about two corrupt police officers in which Tupac starred. It conveys darkness, distrust, and disorientation. The album was released after Tupac's death; reliable public information does not clearly establish the original recording date.
140.details: 2Pac feat. Outlawz | Gang Related: The Soundtrack | Released October 7, 1997, posthumously

141.headline: Missing someone does not mean your life has to stop.
141.fortune: Some people leave, but their absence stays in our lives. Perhaps you have been revisiting someone's memory lately. You do not have to pretend they were perfect to keep loving them. Real relationships contain more than one kind of story. You can mourn and keep living; missing someone is another form of carrying them with you.
141.history: With Stretch, Tupac mourns murdered friends and the wounds they left behind. The song was first issued on Greatest Hits in 1998. The name 'Biggy Smallz' at the recording's beginning refers to someone from his earlier circle; similar spelling alone does not make it a prediction of The Notorious B.I.G.'s 1997 death.
141.details: 2Pac feat. Stretch | Greatest Hits | First released November 24, 1998, posthumously

142.headline: Real love isn't measured in fear
142.fortune: Real affection doesn't demand a daily loyalty test. Maybe you love someone but constantly fear their feelings will change if you aren't successful. Unconditional love doesn't mean tolerating every behavior; it means not measuring a person's worth only by money and status. Notice where you're seen in your relationships and where you're only assessed. Being loved shouldn't be a performance reward.
142.history: A song about love and loyalty, performed by Tupac with Nanci Fletcher's vocals and released on Greatest Hits in 1998. The original vocal was recorded in 1996, while the final version was prepared after his death. Alongside the violent works of the same period, it reveals a gentler, more family-centered side of his outlook.

143.headline: Anger doesn't always get the last word
143.fortune: Anger can make you look invincible for a few minutes. What comes next? Maybe someone insulted you and you want to answer in a way everyone will remember. First ask whether you're looking for a solution or an audience. Some responses echo for years beyond the disagreement itself. Winning a fight doesn't always make life better.
143.history: Tupac's diss track featuring the Outlawz first appeared in 1996 as the companion track to the 'How Do U Want It' single, and later on Greatest Hits. The lyrics directly attack The Notorious B.I.G. and his associates. It is one of the fiercest expressions of the East Coast–West Coast hip-hop conflict of that period.

144.headline: Sometimes you are frightened by who you have become.
144.fortune: You may keep saying 'this is just who I am' to avoid considering change. Living in constant battle mode can create a sense of control while narrowing your choices. Ask which parts of your toughness genuinely protect you and which have become exhausting habits. Not every piece of armor is worth keeping.
144.history: In this violent 1996-era track, Tupac addresses teenage deaths, street conflict, enemies, and nightmares. It received its first widespread release on Greatest Hits in 1998. A central contradiction is that he condemns young people's deaths while continuing to use threats of violence in his own lyrics.
144.details: 2Pac | Greatest Hits | Recorded around 1996; widely released November 24, 1998

145.headline: Nothing changes unless someone wants it to
145.fortune: When everyone says, 'That's just how the world is,' ask yourself who benefits from it staying that way. Maybe you've spent a long time putting up with injustice or an unwritten rule. Change doesn't always begin with a grand decision; sometimes it starts by questioning something everyone considers normal. If something is wrong, being old doesn't make it right.
145.history: Tupac recorded the song years before its release, and the famous version came out posthumously in 1998. A piano sample from Bruce Hornsby's 'The Way It Is' gives life to a protest against racism, poverty, drugs, and police violence. It is among his best-known social and posthumous works.

146.headline: When nobody answers, silence can become injustice.
146.fortune: Perhaps your complaint keeps getting passed between people who refuse responsibility. The anger of not being heard is real, but speaking louder is not always the solution. Name the problem precisely and demand an answer from someone able to change it. A clear protest becomes harder to ignore.
146.history: Opening the 1999 joint album by Tupac and Outlawz, this track addresses the president and structures of power critically. It raises poverty, racism, police pressure, and neglect of disadvantaged communities. Tupac's performance predates his death; the group helped complete the album afterward.
146.details: 2Pac + Outlawz | Still I Rise | Released December 21, 1999, posthumously

147.headline: Your beginnings do not get to define your ending.
147.fortune: You do not have to deny your past to rise above it. Maybe the start of your life was harder than anyone around you understands. Succeeding does not mean erasing your scars; it means still having the right to imagine a future. Early disadvantages are not your entire identity. Falling can be one chapter, not the last.
147.history: The title track of Tupac and Outlawz's joint album, released in December 1999 after his death, moves from childhood poverty and neighborhood pressure toward growth and resilience. Tupac's earlier vocal is combined with performances by group members. Its title celebrates rising despite adversity.
147.details: 2Pac + Outlawz | Still I Rise | Released December 21, 1999, posthumously

148.headline: Loyalty should not be a permanent obedience test.
148.fortune: Some secrets feed on fear more than truth. Maybe everyone around you talks about loyalty, yet no one feels free to say what they think. When trust is measured only through silence and unquestioning agreement, it turns into pressure. Notice what you have hidden from yourself to stay in the group. Friendship should allow honest questions.
148.history: Tupac and Outlawz portray their militant group identity, hidden conflicts, and fierce allegiance. The lyrics are explicitly violent; the title is not practical advice about fighting wars. It appeared on Still I Rise in 1999, using vocals Tupac recorded during his lifetime.
148.details: 2Pac + Outlawz | Still I Rise | Released December 21, 1999, posthumously

149.headline: Crying is not evidence that you are weak.
149.fortune: Sometimes crying means you have not gone numb. Maybe you have begun believing what other people say about you, even when their judgments are unfair. Do not minimize the pain, but do not let those insults become your own voice. Find people around whom you do not need to perform. You are more than their judgment.
149.history: Continuing the themes of 'Keep Ya Head Up,' this song offers reassurance to a woman who has suffered. Tupac's older recording was combined with Outlawz performances and posthumous production. Released on Still I Rise in 1999, it contrasts with the harsher treatment of women in some of his other songs.
149.details: 2Pac + Outlawz | Still I Rise | Released December 21, 1999, posthumously

150.headline: The world does not pause for your pain.
150.fortune: You may have been waiting for a painful event to end before allowing yourself to live again, but days move forward without permission. Time's indifference can be frightening, yet it also creates another chance to choose. You need not forget what happened. You can decide what to carry forward. The clock keeps moving; you do not have to stay behind.
150.history: Tupac and Outlawz describe a turning world shaped by money, murder, prison, and dead friends. Released on Still I Rise in 1999, the song uses earlier Tupac vocals with contributions from the group. Its dark, multi-voice narrative is not a simple optimistic reflection on the passage of time.
150.details: 2Pac + Outlawz | Still I Rise | Released December 21, 1999, posthumously

151.headline: Hope feels different when it understands where you come from.
151.fortune: When someone cannot understand your pain, even your hope searches for a familiar language. Perhaps you need guidance that will not judge you from above, someone who knows what you have endured. Choose role models carefully, but do not let them replace your own thinking. Help begins when the truth of your life is seen.
151.history: In this collaboration, the image of a 'Black Jesus' suggests spiritual refuge close to the experiences of people in marginalized neighborhoods. Tupac and Outlawz move between faith, doubt, violence, and appeals for help. Released on Still I Rise in 1999, its symbolism needs to be read in racial and social context.
151.details: 2Pac + Outlawz | Still I Rise | Released December 21, 1999, posthumously

152.headline: Friendship is built through actions, not slogans.
152.fortune: A real friend does not merely say 'I'm with you.' They stay present when you make mistakes, too. Perhaps one relationship only feels like friendship while everything is easy. Notice the smaller acts: answering calls, checking in, keeping a promise. Then ask when you have fallen short yourself. Loyalty grows through repeated choices.
152.history: Tupac and Outlawz rap about close companions, trust under threat, and street solidarity. The track also ties loyalty to readiness for confrontation, so its picture of friendship is not harmless or purely romantic. It appeared on the 1999 posthumous joint album Still I Rise.
152.details: 2Pac + Outlawz | Still I Rise | Released December 21, 1999, posthumously

153.headline: Running faster will not help if you forgot the destination.
153.fortune: When you are always hustling to survive, you may forget where you hoped to go. Perhaps relentless effort has become a badge of pride while your health and relationships absorb the cost. Ambition is not wrong, but is there still something in your life beyond work and conflict? If the whole road feels like hell, speed is not the answer.
153.history: Tupac and Outlawz describe pressure to earn, street life, prison, and enemies. The lyrics contrast earning money through drugs and through rap, with both depicted amid danger. Released on Still I Rise in 1999, it draws on the aggressive tone of Tupac's later recordings.
153.details: 2Pac + Outlawz | Still I Rise | Released December 21, 1999, posthumously

154.headline: Moving fast can make you miss the next turn.
154.fortune: You want everything immediately: money, success, answers, decisions. Rushing may make you feel ahead, but it also raises the cost of mistakes. Ask yourself whether you are truly behind or merely using somebody else's speed as your measure. Not every road is a race.
154.history: This group track by Tupac and Outlawz evokes a fast-moving life involving substance use, conflict, and risky decisions. Its title suits the relentless motion of their street narrative. It appeared on Still I Rise in 1999, using Tupac's previously recorded performance.
154.details: 2Pac + Outlawz | Still I Rise | Released December 21, 1999, posthumously

155.headline: Some losses have no fair explanation.
155.fortune: When someone dies young, you may search for a reason or someone to blame, hoping the pain will become easier to understand. You do not have to turn every loss into a beautiful lesson. Their memory can live on in what you do for people still here. Mourning is not a contest to find the perfect explanation.
155.history: Tupac and Outlawz address early death, violence, children, and social tragedy. Tupac's lyrics also refer to church burnings, plane crashes, and women's reproductive choices. Released on Still I Rise in 1999, the finalized version may include dedications or references added after his death.
155.details: 2Pac + Outlawz | Still I Rise | Released December 21, 1999, posthumously

156.headline: An independent mind questions both rumors and official stories.
156.fortune: Not everything hidden is a conspiracy, and not everything announced publicly tells the entire truth. Perhaps you are caught between doubt and trust. Asking questions is healthy, but answers need evidence, not just a frightening story's appeal. An independent mind neither believes too quickly nor decides the verdict in advance.
156.history: From Tupac and Outlawz's 1999 Still I Rise collaboration, this confrontational track invokes rivals, power, and the Makaveli identity. 'Killuminati' carries symbolic weight in Tupac's artistic world. The title alone does not prove belief in a specific conspiracy theory or membership in a secret organization.
156.details: 2Pac + Outlawz | Still I Rise | Released December 21, 1999, posthumously

157.headline: Sometimes presence is the only language grief needs.
157.fortune: Some news divides life into a 'before' and 'after.' Maybe you are not ready for a loss, or you feel helpless witnessing someone else's grief. You do not need to find a remarkable sentence. Staying nearby, listening, and remembering can mean more than a thousand pieces of advice. At a time of mourning, being there speaks volumes.
157.history: The title's tears and closed caskets evoke violent deaths and mourning in neighborhoods. Tupac and Outlawz remember lost friends and those who survive them. The album version appeared on Still I Rise in 1999 after Tupac's death and continues the group's collective story of bereavement.
157.details: 2Pac + Outlawz | Still I Rise | Released December 21, 1999, posthumously

158.headline: Some memories are tattooed into your behavior.
158.fortune: An experience can stay with you through the people you choose, the things you fear, and the way you react. You cannot erase the past with a single decision, but you can notice where it still directs your present. Every wound has a story; it does not have to command your future.
158.history: Tupac and Outlawz address pain, loyalty, memories of the dead, and a street identity. A tattooed tear symbolizes grief that lasts and a life marked by violence. The track was released on Still I Rise in 1999, combining Tupac's earlier recording with later final production.
158.details: 2Pac + Outlawz | Still I Rise | Released December 21, 1999, posthumously

159.headline: Nobody is too strong to need protection.
159.fortune: Maybe you are always supporting others and imagine yourself beyond harm. Pride can hide danger, though. Being vulnerable is not a moral failure; it is part of being human. Boundaries, asking for help, and caution also require strength. Do not deny your limits until they take you by surprise.
159.history: The verses are carried mainly by Outlawz members, with Tupac's voice used in the chorus. The theme is that no one is immune to violence and death. The finalized recording also references the losses of Tupac and Kadafi, meaning portions were clearly shaped after their deaths. Released in 1999.
159.details: Outlawz with Tupac vocals | Still I Rise | Released December 21, 1999, posthumously

160.headline: Do not treat your story as finished before its ending.
160.fortune: When you believe the end is close, you may begin making choices as if you have nothing left worth protecting. Yet even amid anger and pressure, tomorrow has not been written. Ask which decision solves a problem only today and what it may cost you later. Your story is not over simply because the present feels dark.
160.history: Opening the posthumous 2001 album Until the End of Time, this song depicts the violent fate of a 'street soldier.' Tupac moves between displays of toughness and awareness of death. His vocal was recorded before September 1996; the released arrangement was completed after his death.
160.details: 2Pac | Until the End of Time | Released March 27, 2001, posthumously; vocals recorded before September 1996

161.headline: One betrayal does not define the whole world.
161.fortune: When trust breaks, you may want to cross friendship off your life entirely. Someone you thought was close has disappointed you, and anger is natural. But condemning every relationship means losing the chance to meet different people. Distance yourself from the one who hurt you, not from the possibility of friendship.
161.history: Tupac attacks opportunistic friends, jealousy, and lost loyalty in sharp language. Its distrust resembles some of his later recordings. Released on Until the End of Time in 2001, the familiar vocal was drawn from older sessions and paired with production completed after his death.
161.details: 2Pac | Until the End of Time | Released March 27, 2001, posthumously

162.headline: Growing up too early is not the same as growing stronger.
162.fortune: Some children become afraid sooner rather than stronger. Perhaps you know a teenager whose aggressive behavior is mistaken for maturity. Behind the pose may be fear of poverty or humiliation. Before passing judgment, consider which opportunities were denied them. No child should have to play a dangerous role to be taken seriously.
162.history: In 'Lil' Homies,' Tupac describes a younger generation growing up under street rules amid guns, money, and violence. The song mixes empathy with depictions of dangerous behavior. It was released posthumously on Until the End of Time in March 2001.
162.details: 2Pac | Until the End of Time | Released March 27, 2001, posthumously

163.headline: The strongest response is not always an immediate one.
163.fortune: Sometimes a harsh reply is exactly what the other person wants. Someone may be pressing every button that makes you angry. Reacting instantly feels powerful, but it can surrender control of the situation. If you want to choose your own actions, put a few seconds between provocation and response. Strength includes knowing when not to strike.
163.history: The Hutch Mix appeared on disc one of Until the End of Time in 2001. Its themes are rivalry, threats, and retaliation. Tupac's voice comes from pre-death recordings, with new production for the album. A Committee Mix also exists in the set, but the two are treated here as one song.
163.details: 2Pac | Until the End of Time | Hutch Mix released March 27, 2001, posthumously

164.headline: Living well is different from looking successful.
164.fortune: Maybe you fought hard for money and comfort, and now want everyone to see what you achieved. Before buying another symbol of success, ask what genuinely makes your days better. Comfort matters, but if peace is forever postponed, so is enjoyment. A good life is not simply one that looks impressive from outside.
164.history: Working with other artists, Tupac describes money, achievement, and dreams of escaping economic hardship. The image of a better life combines experiences of deprivation with hip-hop's culture of displaying wealth in the 1990s. The track appeared posthumously on Until the End of Time in 2001.
164.details: 2Pac | Until the End of Time | Released March 27, 2001, posthumously

165.headline: The most valuable inheritance may be honesty.
165.fortune: Sometimes we write words for someone who cannot hear them yet. Maybe you want to pass experience to the next generation but do not know how to begin. Your story does not need to be flawless; mistakes can teach too. If someone follows your path one day, what should they know? An inheritance is not only money.
165.history: Addressing a child who has not yet been born, Tupac reflects on his past, danger, responsibility, and hopes for a better future. The imagined addressee is a poetic device, not proof that Tupac had a child when he recorded it. Released posthumously in 2001, it became an album single.
165.details: 2Pac | Until the End of Time | Released March 27, 2001, posthumously

166.headline: Breathing and truly living are not the same.
166.fortune: Maybe your world is full of pressure and competition, and you feel you must prove every minute that you are not falling behind. Yet a step taken only out of fear may not move you forward. Ask why you are running and where you actually want to go. Sometimes another breath is reason enough not to rush.
166.history: With Outlawz, Tupac describes survival amid danger, enemies, and the relentless rhythm of street life. The title points to continuing to breathe despite threats. His earlier vocal was used for the version released on the 2001 posthumous album Until the End of Time.
166.details: 2Pac feat. Outlawz | Until the End of Time | Released March 27, 2001, posthumously

167.headline: A safe home is more than four walls.
167.fortune: Maybe you have been searching for a place where you no longer need to stay on guard. Sometimes that home begins with a relationship where someone actually listens. But wanting peace is not enough; building it takes different actions. A happy home grows through what you do, not only what you promise.
167.history: Tupac longs for a peaceful home and lasting relationship away from violent street life. He also imagines a future child and worries about passing on a father's suffering. Released on Until the End of Time in 2001, the song's narrative should not automatically be treated as documented facts about his family life.
167.details: 2Pac | Until the End of Time | Released March 27, 2001, posthumously

168.headline: Going all out is not always courage.
168.fortune: Maybe you decided to fight to the end, even though the original reason barely matters now. Before spending every ounce of energy proving a point, ask what the possible result is worth. Persistence is good when the purpose remains clear. When anger is all that remains, changing direction may take greater strength.
168.history: Featuring Outlawz, the song describes relentless conflict, enemies, and the collective Outlaw identity. Its tone is violent and aggressive; the fortune offers an independent reflection on that tension. Tupac recorded his part before his death, though precise session details are not firmly established.
168.details: 2Pac feat. Outlawz | Until the End of Time | Released March 27, 2001, posthumously

169.headline: Confidence does not have to shout.
169.fortune: Some people try to frighten you simply by making you believe they are dangerous. Maybe you are caught in a rivalry where every small exchange sounds like a threat. You do not have to imitate that language to protect your dignity. There is a difference between setting a boundary and starting another war. Walk away when the cost is too high.
169.history: Tupac addresses enemies who, in his telling, chose the 'wrong' person to challenge. Threats and street violence dominate the lyrics. The track appeared on disc one of Until the End of Time in 2001, using a vocal recorded earlier in his career.
169.details: 2Pac | Until the End of Time | Released March 27, 2001, posthumously

170.headline: Shared wounds do not guarantee a safe relationship.
170.fortune: When two people have been hurt in similar ways, they can feel close very quickly. But understanding each other's pain is not enough to create trust. Maybe you both still carry old anger. Look at what you are building together, not merely what happened to you before. Mutual understanding is a beginning, not a guarantee.
170.history: The Jamie Mix of 'Thug N U Thug N Me' appears on disc one of Until the End of Time. It connects closeness, 'thug' identity, and street lifestyle. Another arrangement appears on disc two; both are treated as versions of one track rather than separate fortunes.
170.details: 2Pac | Until the End of Time | Jamie Mix released March 27, 2001, posthumously

171.headline: Some debts cannot be paid with money.
171.fortune: Maybe you believe someone stole something that never came back: an opportunity, respect, or years of your life. Seeking justice is different from seeking revenge, though the boundary can feel blurry. Ask whether you want real repair or simply want someone else to suffer. Settling accounts without a goal can become another prison.
171.history: Tupac addresses the history of oppression and demands redress for Black Americans. Unlike many confrontational songs on the album, the subject is not merely a personal enemy but a historical, social injustice. It appeared posthumously on Until the End of Time in 2001.
171.details: 2Pac | Until the End of Time | Released March 27, 2001, posthumously

172.headline: Big promises face big tests
172.fortune: The promise 'for the rest of my life' is beautiful, but people change along the way. Maybe you're still loyal to a relationship, an idea, or an image of yourself formed years ago. Loyalty matters, yet you can ask what should stay and what has the right to change. Staying true to your values doesn't always mean staying the same person.
172.history: The title track of the 2001 posthumous album finds Tupac speaking about friendship, fame, people changing, and loyalty until the end. The song also draws on pop and R&B sounds and is connected with the Outlawz. The RP Remix is a version of the same song and is not numbered as another fortune in this collection.
172.details: 2Pac | Until the End of Time | Released 2001

173.headline: Not every account can be settled in cash.
173.fortune: When money becomes the measure of everything, relationships begin to have price tags too. Perhaps you are judging every person by profit and loss because you fear ending up with nothing. Financial caution matters, but seeing every feeling as weakness costs you things money cannot buy.
173.history: Here M.O.B. invokes placing money above relationships within street culture. With members of Thug Life and Outlawz, Tupac raps about weapons, prison, wealth, and demeaning depictions of women. Released in 2001, the song's misogyny is part of the text, not an attitude endorsed by this fortune.
173.details: 2Pac | Until the End of Time | Released March 27, 2001, posthumously

174.headline: A larger circle does not always mean less loneliness.
174.fortune: Maybe you know more people than ever, yet cannot think of whom to call on a hard day. A large group can feel powerful, but genuine connection takes understanding and trust. Do not measure the worth of a community solely by its size or noise. One reliable companion can matter more than a hundred voices agreeing.
174.history: Featuring artists close to Tupac, this track portrays a broad network of street groups bound by a shared identity. Its tone is boastful and rooted in group loyalty. It closes disc one of Until the End of Time, released after Tupac's death in March 2001.
174.details: 2Pac | Until the End of Time | Released March 27, 2001, posthumously

175.headline: Your closest friend is a history, not a title.
175.fortune: The people who truly stayed beside you may not be the ones who speak the loudest. Perhaps you overlook quiet companions in a busy life. Do not measure friendship by messages or group photos; one person may show up in danger when everyone else disappears. Ask whether you have been that kind of companion for someone.
175.history: On disc two of Until the End of Time, this song focuses on close friends, loyalty under threat, and street identity. Its language and images are often violent. Tupac's vocals predate his death, while the released arrangement belongs to the 2001 posthumous album.
175.details: 2Pac | Until the End of Time | Released March 27, 2001, posthumously

176.headline: A harmful habit is not a law of nature.
176.fortune: Sometimes 'that's just who I am' becomes an excuse to avoid change. Perhaps someone keeps hurting you and asks you to accept it as their nature. Differences in personality are real, but they do not cancel responsibility for behavior. People can be complicated and still answer for their choices.
176.history: A rearranged version featuring Lil' Mo appeared on disc two of the 2001 album. Tupac discusses romantic and sexual relationships through ideas about the 'nature' of street-minded men. The lyrics contain gender stereotypes and degrading language; this fortune does not treat those claims as universal truths.
176.details: 2Pac feat. Lil' Mo | Until the End of Time | Remix released March 27, 2001, posthumously

177.headline: Even someone feared by everyone can cry at night.
177.fortune: Maybe you have hidden sadness behind anger for years because you expect nobody to take it seriously. But pain does not vanish when concealed; sometimes it only emerges in harsher forms. You do not have to keep playing someone without feelings. Tears are not a defeat for your pride. They are part of being alive.
177.history: Tupac addresses grief within violent street life, a fascination with danger, shootings, and the cost of rivalry. The contrast between a 'thug' image and human vulnerability lies at the song's heart. The earlier vocal was released on the posthumous Until the End of Time album in 2001.
177.details: 2Pac | Until the End of Time | Released March 27, 2001, posthumously

178.headline: Trust is earned through actions, not reassurances.
178.fortune: Whenever someone says 'don't worry,' ask yourself what you might reasonably be worried about. Some reassurances are sincere; others ask you to follow without questions. Perhaps you want to trust someone but their actions tell another story. Good trust matches what a person does, not just what they promise.
178.history: Tupac opens the song by urging a companion into a car while minimizing fears of gunfire. He then moves into threats against enemies and group loyalty. Its title therefore sounds inside a dangerous situation rather than promising real safety. Released on Until the End of Time in 2001.
178.details: 2Pac | Until the End of Time | Released March 27, 2001, posthumously

179.headline: If every day is only survival, ask what living would mean.
179.fortune: Perhaps your routine has become work, worry, and starting all over again. Survival matters, but you are allowed to want more than getting through the next crisis. One genuine small change is worth more than grand slogans. Your life should not become merely the space between two emergencies.
179.history: The track describes stress, violence, and a life constrained by street rules. Its title, 'This Ain't Livin,' signals exhaustion with those conditions, even as the lyrics continue in a harsh, threatening style. It was released posthumously on Until the End of Time in 2001.
179.details: 2Pac | Until the End of Time | Released March 27, 2001, posthumously

180.headline: Old trust does not grant permission for new harm.
180.fortune: The bitterest distance is sometimes between you and someone who once stood beside you. Maybe you are still asking why they changed. Some answers will never come from the other person. You can judge people by how they behave today even when yesterday's memories are precious. Past closeness does not require you to accept fresh betrayal.
180.history: Tupac confronts people who once seemed friendly but turned against him, expressing anger over betrayal. A disc-two track from Until the End of Time, it was released in March 2001. The threatening lyrics combine the pain of betrayal with a desire for revenge.
180.details: 2Pac | Until the End of Time | Released March 27, 2001, posthumously

181.headline: Being the last one left does not mean you have reached the end.
181.fortune: Maybe the group you once relied on has grown smaller, leaving you to make difficult decisions alone. You can honor those who are gone without handing every choice to your memories of them. Being the last person standing does not mean there is no road ahead.
181.history: Featuring Outlawz, this track speaks of companions who survived danger and rivalry, using boasts and threats. It appeared on disc two of Until the End of Time in 2001. Tupac's performance predates his death, but the exact recording session remains uncertain.
181.details: 2Pac feat. Outlawz | Until the End of Time | Released March 27, 2001, posthumously

182.headline: An inheritance is not only something you can spend.
182.fortune: Some words are written for someone who has not yet entered your life. Maybe you think about the future and fear that your old mistakes could be repeated. You cannot control the next generation's entire path, but you can leave them something valuable: honesty about what you experienced. That, too, is an inheritance.
182.history: Tupac addresses an imagined future child from the viewpoint of a potential father, discussing poverty, injustice, prison, and fear of passing on violence. Unlike purely aggressive tracks, this one looks toward the next generation. The version featuring Nutso appeared on Until the End of Time in 2001.
182.details: 2Pac feat. Nutso | Until the End of Time | Released March 27, 2001, posthumously

183.headline: Courage will not fill an empty tank.
183.fortune: A person who always pushes to the limit can suddenly run out of strength. Maybe you demand constant movement from yourself and treat every sign of fatigue as failure. What is all that running for? Sometimes a short stop is the only way to make your next decision clearly. Even bravery needs something to run on.
183.history: The title refers to moving with an almost empty fuel tank. Tupac and his collaborators address the pressures of street life, substance use, scarce resources, and danger, not simply the need to rest. Released on disc two of the posthumous Until the End of Time album in 2001.
183.details: 2Pac | Until the End of Time | Released March 27, 2001, posthumously

184.headline: A comeback matters, but so does its direction.
184.fortune: People expect you to slow down after surviving a crisis. Yet you might feel a new urgency to prove yourself. Make sure success is not just a response to others who humiliated you. Decide what you are moving toward, not only whom you are fighting against. Returning is meaningful when the direction is your own.
184.history: A reworked recording featuring Trick Daddy was released on Better Dayz in 2002. Tupac addresses being shot, prison, dead friends, and keeping going despite danger. The track's tone is confrontational and violent, not purely motivational.
184.details: 2Pac feat. Trick Daddy | Better Dayz | Released November 26, 2002, posthumously

185.headline: Not every opponent deserves to become an enemy.
185.fortune: Maybe you have been replaying an old conflict over and over, as though you owe it a final answer. Anger may be justified, but what would retaliation actually give you? Some victories only deepen a wound. You do not have to turn every disagreement into a war.
185.history: Tupac attacks rivals and threatens street revenge in this diss track. A Briss remix appeared on Better Dayz in 2002. His original vocal was recorded during his lifetime, while the released arrangement was completed after his death.
185.details: 2Pac | Better Dayz | Briss Remix released November 26, 2002, posthumously

186.headline: Change is something you do, not something you announce.
186.fortune: Saying 'I am not that person anymore' does not prove anything. Maybe someone is asking you for another chance, or you want to move beyond your own past. Look at repeated behavior rather than one evening's promises. Change is possible, but it takes time and responsibility. A new person is built through new decisions.
186.history: Tupac presents a supposedly changed man alongside ambition, wealth, and street competition. The 2002 album version was rearranged with Jazze Pha, T.I., and Johnta Austin. Their appearances on Better Dayz do not mean they recorded with Tupac in person.
186.details: 2Pac feat. Jazze Pha, T.I. & Johnta Austin | Better Dayz | Released November 26, 2002, posthumously

187.headline: One broken relationship does not condemn everyone.
187.fortune: Maybe you want to give up on everybody because expecting loyalty has become exhausting. People may have talked behind your back or left you alone. Taking distance is your right, but the claim that 'nobody is trustworthy' makes your world smaller. Judge people individually. Pain from one relationship does not have to become a permanent verdict on all others.
187.history: Tupac lashes out at enemies, critics, and those he believed wanted to bring him down. The performance is linked with Outlawz and filled with threats and insults. The final version appeared after his death on Better Dayz in 2002.
187.details: 2Pac feat. Outlawz | Better Dayz | Released November 26, 2002, posthumously

188.headline: Peace without justice does not last long.
188.fortune: Being told to calm down is not much comfort when the danger remains. Maybe people expect your silence without addressing the problem that hurts you. Real peace also requires being heard and changing circumstances. You have the right to name the problem even when others would rather ignore it. Quiet alone is not justice.
188.history: Tupac says he wants peace but finds it out of reach amid poverty, violence among young people, and insecurity. The 2002 Better Dayz version features E.D.I. and Kastro. The lyrics contrast a desire for peace with carrying weapons for self-defense.
188.details: 2Pac feat. E.D.I. & Kastro | Better Dayz | Released November 26, 2002, posthumously

189.headline: Some adults were never allowed to be children.
189.fortune: Before judging a mother's choices, remember how young she may have been when hardship arrived. Perhaps you see someone only through their mistakes and not the burdens placed on them too soon. Understanding the past does not undo the harm, but it can make judgment more humane. Some grown-ups never had much of a childhood.
189.history: The song follows a very young mother confronting loss, poverty, pregnancy, and violence. Tupac looks beyond her responsibility to the social conditions around her. A version featuring Kimmy Hill appeared on Better Dayz in 2002. The narrative is not necessarily his own mother's biography.
189.details: 2Pac feat. Kimmy Hill | Better Dayz | Released November 26, 2002, posthumously

190.headline: A big name does not guarantee freedom.
190.fortune: It can be easy to become known for something and hard to control what that reputation means. Maybe you built a persona to gain respect and now feel exhausted carrying it. Give yourself permission to be seen beyond old labels. Your past can be famous without owning your future.
190.history: This solo Tupac recording is distinct from the Thug Life song of the same title discussed earlier in the collection. A Briss remix appeared on Better Dayz in 2002. The lyrics focus on street fame, money, rivalry, and the danger of being watched.
190.details: 2Pac | Better Dayz | Briss Remix released November 26, 2002, posthumously

191.headline: The hard decision is louder than the loud boast.
191.fortune: Anyone can sound brave while talking. Maybe today you have to show what lies behind your claims. You need not enter a fight to prove you mean business. Sometimes action means setting a boundary and refusing a dangerous game. Courage is measured by the decision, not the volume of the threat.
191.history: Featuring Outlawz members, the track appeared on Better Dayz with a threatening, combative tone. It centers on facing rivals and group loyalty. Tupac's part was recorded before 1996, but the 2002 album mix should not automatically be treated as his intended final arrangement.
191.details: 2Pac feat. Outlawz | Better Dayz | Released November 26, 2002, posthumously

192.headline: Fairness cannot survive without honesty.
192.fortune: When a relationship starts to resemble a transaction, somebody usually pays more than they expected. Perhaps you want something returned but have never discussed what you each expect. A clear agreement is different from a hidden ledger. Ask openly what both of you want. Fair exchange requires understanding rather than unspoken debts.
192.history: Tupac discusses sex and exchanging benefits using explicit and at times objectifying language. Better Dayz includes a version featuring Jazze Pha and another arrangement involving Mýa. Both versions are treated as one track here, released in 2002.
192.details: 2Pac | Better Dayz | Versions released November 26, 2002, posthumously

193.headline: Not every late-night choice looks good in daylight.
193.fortune: Tonight's excitement can make tomorrow's costs seem unreal. Maybe the crowd and the moment have made a risky choice feel ordinary. There is nothing wrong with having fun, but when other people's energy takes over your judgment, choosing freely becomes harder. Not every invitation needs an immediate yes.
193.history: This track is associated with parties, late-night encounters, brief relationships, and risky living. It first appeared on the 1999 compilation Chronic 2000 and was included on some editions of Better Dayz in 2002. It may be absent from certain newer digital track lists.
193.details: 2Pac | First released on Chronic 2000 in 1999; appeared on some 2002 Better Dayz editions

194.headline: Not every star starts somewhere bright.
194.fortune: Maybe you came from a place other people describe only through its shortages. That background can motivate you, but you should not have to romanticize its hardships to prove your worth. You can rise from difficult surroundings while being honest about their damage. Shining does not erase the darkness you left behind.
194.history: Tupac and Nutso explore becoming a star from a disadvantaged neighborhood, alongside money and street credibility. The released version appeared on Better Dayz in 2002. Stardom is linked with displays of power and danger, not a straightforward story of healthy success.
194.details: 2Pac feat. Nutso | Better Dayz | Released November 26, 2002, posthumously

195.headline: Maybe you just need somewhere safe
195.fortune: Maybe what you're searching for isn't more success, just somewhere safe. A place where you don't have to explain why you're tired or be ready to defend yourself every moment. Ask yourself where, and with whom, you can truly feel at peace. Sometimes the biggest dream is one night without worry.
195.history: Tupac imagines a place of peace for people who have lived under the pressure of poverty, shootings, and death. An acoustic version with Nas and another version with Anthony Hamilton appeared on Better Dayz in 2002; both rework the same song. Its references to death and suffering are serious.

196.headline: Belonging somewhere does not mean you have to stay.
196.fortune: Some streets stay with you even after you leave. Maybe your old neighborhood holds both cherished memories and reasons you wanted to escape. You do not have to deny either. You can love your roots while wanting a different life. Belonging is not a sentence to remain.
196.history: Tupac remembers his neighborhood, children, poverty, violence, and the experience of growing up within limits. An early version appeared in the 1995 documentary The Show; a reworked Nitty remix appeared on Better Dayz in 2002. Both count here as versions of one work.
196.details: 2Pac | First released on The Show soundtrack in 1995; Nitty Remix released on Better Dayz in 2002

197.headline: Words can outlive the argument that caused them.
197.fortune: Maybe someone has told you 'don't take it seriously, I was angry.' But respect does not return through apology alone. If you truly withdraw a hurtful word, your later behavior should show it. People live with the effects of what we say, not only what we meant to say.
197.history: Tupac reflects on how he addresses women and the tension between anger and respect. The 2002 Better Dayz version features Tyrese. Its meaning becomes more complicated alongside tracks where he insults women; that contradiction is an important part of the record.
197.details: 2Pac feat. Tyrese | Better Dayz | Released November 26, 2002, posthumously

198.headline: Better days begin today
198.fortune: Better days don't start by denying today. Maybe you're tired of everyone saying, 'It'll be fine,' while the problem is still right in front of you. Hope is serious when it addresses the causes of hardship and does something to change them. You don't have to fix everything yourself, but you can choose your part. Hope isn't another name for forgetting.
198.history: On the title track of the 2002 album, Tupac speaks about drugs, murder, poverty, prison, and hope for a safer neighborhood. The album version was released with Mr. Biggs's vocals. Despite its hopefulness, the track doesn't offer a simplified or sanitized picture of street life.

199.headline: Having a number is not the same as having someone to call.
199.fortune: Maybe you have plenty of company on good days but still do not know whom to call when life gets difficult. Closeness is more than sending invitations; it means checking in and showing up. Someone who reliably stands beside you rarely needs to promise it every day.
199.history: With a romantic and seductive tone, Tupac invites someone to contact him and meet up. The Jazze Pha remix appeared on Better Dayz in 2002. The lyrics are mainly about attraction and relationships, while this fortune broadens the idea of calling someone toward genuine trust.
199.details: 2Pac | Better Dayz | Jazze Pha Remix released November 26, 2002, posthumously

200.headline: A mind that sees only enemies misses possible solutions.
200.fortune: When you view everything as war, even friendship starts looking like a trench. Maybe you have begun interpreting every disagreement as a threat. Being firm sometimes matters, but attack and defense are not your only options. Before responding, identify the actual issue. Constantly searching for enemies makes solutions harder to see.
200.history: Featuring Buckshot and Cocoa Brovaz, this East Coast-West Coast collaboration is associated with Tupac's proposed One Nation project. It uses military language to address drug policy, incarceration, and street struggle. The released version appeared on Better Dayz in 2002.
200.details: 2Pac feat. Buckshot & Cocoa Brovaz | Better Dayz | Released November 26, 2002, posthumously

201.headline: Being seen is not the same as being known.
201.fortune: Fame brings more voices into your life, not necessarily more accurate ones. Maybe people notice you now and you feel responsible for answering every rumor. You do not need to make each stranger's opinion part of your identity. Ask which outside voices actually help you grow.
201.history: Tupac and Outlawz describe fame, jealousy, media attention, and the pressures of success. A rearranged version appeared on Better Dayz in 2002. Its suspicious view of celebrity's costs reflects the performers' perspective, not an impartial assessment of everyone around Tupac.
201.details: 2Pac feat. Outlawz | Better Dayz | Released November 26, 2002, posthumously

202.headline: Chosen silence is not always surrender.
202.fortune: When your feelings are provoked, you may make a decision that does not even feel like yours. Perhaps someone has challenged your pride and is waiting for a reaction. Anger does not always deserve an instant response. Before letting someone else's provocation move you, ask who controls the situation.
202.history: This Outlawz group track addresses rivalry, sensitivity to disrespect, and violent reactions in street culture. Released on Better Dayz in 2002, it uses an earlier Tupac performance. The fortune draws on the colloquial phrase 'catching feelings,' not on explicit advice in the lyrics.
202.details: 2Pac feat. Outlawz | Better Dayz | Released November 26, 2002, posthumously

203.headline: An open door can reveal a missing boundary.
203.fortune: Someone who returns again and again may not be coming back to stay. Perhaps a relationship restarts with fresh promises and ends with the same old problem. Rather than guessing intentions, watch patterns of behavior. Genuine change leaves evidence. Keeping the door open is not always an act of hope.
203.history: With Outlawz members, Tupac describes attraction, sexual relationships, and distrust. The Better Dayz version appeared in 2002 with contributions from Jazze Pha and others. Parts of the lyrics are misogynistic; this fortune does not treat those lines as relationship advice.
203.details: 2Pac feat. Outlawz | Better Dayz | Released November 26, 2002, posthumously

204.headline: Old habits are not destiny.
204.fortune: When you play one role for years, you may forget that other choices exist. Perhaps the image people have of you has begun to narrow your life. Ask which parts you genuinely want and which you keep only to protect your reputation. Habit can feel inevitable without being permanent.
204.history: Tupac and Outlawz portray a dangerous lifestyle of loyalty, money, and violence. Released on Better Dayz in 2002, the track brings together personal choices and environmental pressure. Its first-person lyrics should not be mistaken for a complete factual account of Tupac's private life.
204.details: 2Pac feat. Outlawz | Better Dayz | Released November 26, 2002, posthumously

205.headline: Trust is tested by behavior, not promises.
205.fortune: When you suspect everyone, even your own voice can start to sound unfamiliar. Maybe painful experiences have made every promise seem worthless. Blind trust is dangerous, but total distrust shuts doors too. Look for people whose actions have been consistent, not merely convincing. Faith in another person grows through what they do.
205.history: Tupac and Kadafi ask questions about faith, mortality, fate, insecurity, and trust. The song circulated on another collection before its 2002 Better Dayz album version. Its lyrics move between spiritual searching and fear-filled, violent imagery.
205.details: 2Pac feat. Kadafi | Better Dayz | Album version released November 26, 2002

206.headline: Powerful indifference is part of the problem.
206.fortune: When people tell you to be patient, you have the right to ask for how long. Perhaps you have described an injustice repeatedly while those capable of changing it remain unmoved. Protest is more than releasing anger; it should identify what is wrong and what needs to change. Indifference from people in power has consequences.
206.history: Tupac and Outlawz protest social inequality, police mistreatment, and government neglect of disadvantaged neighborhoods. The released version appeared on Better Dayz in 2002, using Tupac's earlier recording. Its title expresses political anger rather than an impartial account of every institution.
206.details: 2Pac feat. Outlawz | Better Dayz | Released November 26, 2002, posthumously

207.headline: Living in memory is not the same as living in the past.
207.fortune: Sometimes a person who has gone remains more vivid than many people still here. Perhaps someone absent continues to shape your decisions. You can preserve their memory without having to relive their absence each day. Carrying someone with you does not require standing still.
207.history: Produced in a version by Eminem, 'Ghost' was released on the 2003 documentary soundtrack Tupac: Resurrection, using older Tupac vocals. It addresses his hard-edged identity and the lingering image others hold of him. It was not a new message written after his death.
207.details: 2Pac | Tupac: Resurrection soundtrack | Released November 2003, posthumously

208.headline: You do not have to solve your whole life tonight.
208.fortune: Maybe you have been staring so hard at the end of the road that you cannot see your next step. Turn one overwhelming problem into a decision you can make today without pretending the difficulty is small. When the path is dark, you do not need to see all of it. Sometimes today is enough.
208.history: The 'Em's Version' on the 2003 Tupac: Resurrection soundtrack combines older Tupac material with performances by Eminem and Outlawz. The lyrics address street pressure, death, and persistence. Its final arrangement was assembled after Tupac died, not through an in-person session with Eminem.
208.details: 2Pac with Eminem and Outlawz | Tupac: Resurrection soundtrack | Released November 2003, posthumously

209.headline: Sometimes you have to stop running
209.fortune: If you're running all day, stop once to ask what you're running from. Maybe you've been in such a hurry to save yourself that you haven't noticed which fear still follows you. Sometimes the circumstances need to change; sometimes your way of seeing them does. Aimless running won't solve either. Finding a way out begins with recognizing the danger.
209.history: Combining recorded vocals by Tupac and The Notorious B.I.G. with production by Eminem, this track appeared on the 2003 documentary soundtrack. It addresses violence, death, and life under pressure. The final combination was made after both rappers had died, rather than being a new collaboration between them.

210.headline: A familiar name does not guarantee familiar intentions.
210.fortune: Some battles are continued by other people in your name. Maybe someone is using your words or image to settle a score you never chose. Before taking a side, separate what the person actually said from what others later built around them. A recognizable name is not proof of a recognizable purpose.
