210.history: The 2003 Tupac: Resurrection release combines an older Tupac vocal with a verse by 50 Cent. The added section refers to rap rivalries of the early 2000s. It should not be treated as Tupac personally taking a side in disputes that arose after his death.
210.details: 2Pac feat. 50 Cent | Tupac: Resurrection soundtrack | Released November 2003, posthumously

211.headline: Even a soldier deserves to put down the shield.
211.fortune: When you have fought just to survive, peace can begin to feel unfamiliar. Maybe you no longer allow yourself to be vulnerable because you fear losing your tough image. You do not need to prove every day that you can withstand everything. A strong person also has the right to rest.
211.history: Produced in a version by Eminem and Luis Resto, this song reworks older Tupac recordings and also bears the title 'Return of the Soulja.' Released on Loyal to the Game in 2004, it uses military imagery and a threatening street-soldier persona.
211.details: 2Pac | Loyal to the Game | Released December 14, 2004, posthumously

212.headline: Not every final blow ends the argument.
212.fortune: A sharp remark may have provoked you, and now you want the last word. Before responding, ask whether you are seeking respect or simply want the other person to suffer. Some answers only push a conflict one step further. Landing the last blow is not necessarily the same as solving the problem.
212.history: Tupac, alongside Outlawz vocals, describes striking rivals and demonstrating street superiority. Produced for the final version by Eminem, the track appeared on Loyal to the Game in 2004. Its language includes explicit metaphors and images of violence.
212.details: 2Pac with Outlawz | Loyal to the Game | Released December 14, 2004, posthumously

213.headline: An open door does not guarantee a wise exit.
213.fortune: Freedom can be only a few steps away from repeating the mistake that cost you so much. Maybe you have just left a period of restriction and want to make up for everything at once. A second chance matters when it brings different choices. A door opening is not proof that you are heading the right way.
213.history: Tupac raps about release on bail, legal pressure, money, and life under scrutiny. An older recording was reconstructed with new production for Loyal to the Game in 2004. Its first-person story should not automatically be matched to a specific date in his legal history without evidence.
213.details: 2Pac | Loyal to the Game | Released December 14, 2004, posthumously

214.headline: Before judging, see the world through their eyes
214.fortune: Before judging the next generation, look at the world you've left them. You may be angry at younger people's behavior while overlooking the fears and failures surrounding them. Blame alone doesn't bring change. Sometimes the right question isn't, 'Why did they turn out this way?' but, 'What did we give them?'
214.history: On this song, Tupac speaks about violence, racism, young people, and a wish for peace. The 2004 version, produced by Eminem, uses parts of Elton John's music and was released on Loyal to the Game. The verses and final arrangement belong to two different periods.

215.headline: Your identity is more than the label people gave you.
215.fortune: If you do not know the story of your roots, someone else can more easily tell it for you. Maybe lately you hear only outside labels describing who you are. Learn the past carefully, not to remain inside it but to recognize how it still shapes today. Your history deserves your own understanding.
215.history: Referring to slavery, race, and the oppression of Black Americans, the song reflects Tupac's political voice. The 2004 Loyal to the Game version combines older Tupac vocals with Eminem and Outlawz contributions. The original performance was recorded years before his death.
215.details: 2Pac with Eminem and Outlawz | Loyal to the Game | Released December 14, 2004, posthumously

216.headline: Loyalty without conscience is complicity.
216.fortune: Loyalty becomes difficult when staying may harm you. Perhaps you are expected to back a person or group even when they do something wrong. Worthwhile loyalty includes honesty, not looking away. Ask whether you remain loyal to a person as they are now or to an image you formed long ago. Friendship cannot excuse everything.
216.history: The 2004 album version features G-Unit members alongside older Tupac vocals. Its title evokes loyalty to street codes; a DJ Quik arrangement also appeared separately. Both releases count here as versions of one song rather than distinct tracks.
216.details: 2Pac feat. G-Unit | Loyal to the Game | Released December 14, 2004, posthumously

217.headline: Loneliness can happen in a crowded room.
217.fortune: Someone surrounded by people may feel lonelier than anyone. Perhaps you always play the strong one in a group, and nobody notices how tired you are. Being physically close to others is not the same as feeling seen. One honest conversation can mean more than a dozen appearances together. Loneliness does not require an empty room.
217.history: The song reveals loneliness and emotion beneath the hard street persona. The 2004 Loyal to the Game release features Nate Dogg with Tupac's older vocals. The tension between projecting power and longing for closeness gives the track its distinct character.
217.details: 2Pac feat. Nate Dogg | Loyal to the Game | Released December 14, 2004, posthumously

218.headline: A new name cannot do the work for you.
218.fortune: Names can give you a sense of power, but they change nothing by themselves. Maybe you have built a new identity and want other people to take it seriously. Identity becomes meaningful through your actions and decisions. No title can replace walking the road you chose.
218.history: The title recasts a U.S. racial slur as an acronym, 'Never Ignorant About Getting Goals Accomplished.' Tupac discusses success, goals, and street identity. The version with Jadakiss appeared on Loyal to the Game in 2004; its featured-artist combination was assembled after Tupac's death.
218.details: 2Pac feat. Jadakiss | Loyal to the Game | Released December 14, 2004, posthumously

219.headline: Saying you love something is easier than choosing it.
219.fortune: Maybe you are caught between what you truly want and what others expect of you. Not every attachment deserves your peace of mind. Ask yourself what kind of person the relationship or desire is turning you into. The heart often sees more clearly when the eyes stay open too.
219.history: Released on Loyal to the Game in 2004, this Tupac song moves between romance, sexual attraction, and street lifestyle. The fortune is an independent reflection on emotional choices, not a direct moral ruling expressed by the artist in his lyrics.
219.details: 2Pac | Loyal to the Game | Released December 14, 2004, posthumously

220.headline: Suspicion is not evidence.
220.fortune: When you assume everyone is dishonest, you may start acting the same way just to strike first. Maybe painful experiences have taught you to be constantly ready for conflict. Self-defense matters, but not every choice driven by suspicion is sound. Ask what you can actually prove and what is merely an old memory speaking.
220.history: Tupac raps about street life, distrust, and the persona of a 'crooked' man confronting rivals. Both the main version and a Raphael Saadiq remix appeared on Loyal to the Game in 2004. They are treated as one track here to avoid duplication.
220.details: 2Pac | Loyal to the Game | Album and Raphael Saadiq remix released December 14, 2004

221.headline: Without conversation, trust cannot survive.
221.fortune: Fear of betrayal can destroy a relationship before betrayal ever happens. Maybe you keep searching for proof that someone is lying. Blind trust is unnecessary, but constant interrogation does not create closeness. If something is troubling you, say it plainly instead of setting hidden tests. Trust needs honest conversation.
221.history: The song addresses suspicion, romantic tension, and distrust. Its 2004 Loyal to the Game version used new production around previously recorded Tupac vocals. The relationship in the lyrics is a dramatic narrative, not evidence of a particular romance in his life.
221.details: 2Pac | Loyal to the Game | Released December 14, 2004, posthumously

222.headline: Temporary relief is not the same as solving the problem.
222.fortune: Some habits look more like temporary shelters when seen from the outside. Maybe after every difficult day you return to something that quiets your thoughts for a few hours. But feeling calmer briefly does not mean the underlying problem has disappeared. If you have found a way to escape pressure, you may still need a way to address it.
222.history: Tupac links drinking, friendship, pleasure, and the pressure of street life. Loyal to the Game contains a 2004 version featuring Obie Trice and a Red Spyda remix. Those arrangements are two releases of the same song, not two independent stories.
222.details: 2Pac feat. Obie Trice | Loyal to the Game | Album version and Red Spyda remix released December 14, 2004

223.headline: Identity becomes a cage when it leaves no room to grow.
223.fortune: 'I'll always be this way' can express loyalty or fear of changing. Maybe you resist growth because it feels like betraying your past and friends. But honoring your roots is not the same as repeating every old choice. An identity worth keeping should have room for the person you are becoming.
223.history: Tupac links himself to the Thug Life identity, emphasizing endurance, street credibility, and the life he knows. A newly produced version was released on Loyal to the Game in 2004. The title and tone stress steadfastness, even where that becomes limiting.
223.details: 2Pac | Loyal to the Game | Released December 14, 2004, posthumously

224.headline: Poverty is not only a lack of money; it is a lack of choices.
224.fortune: When paying for today consumes every thought, making plans for tomorrow can feel like a luxury. Perhaps you expect someone to make a 'reasonable' choice without seeing how many options were already closed to them. Do not judge too quickly. A person struggling to survive does not start from the same place as someone comfortable.
224.history: Tupac addresses poverty, inequality, and economic pressures experienced by Black Americans. A Scott Storch remix with Ron Isley appeared on Loyal to the Game in 2004. Its social concerns recall the political themes of Tupac's earliest recordings.
224.details: 2Pac feat. Ron Isley | Loyal to the Game | Scott Storch Remix released December 14, 2004

225.headline: Nobody is untouchable simply because they say so.
225.fortune: Someone who insists they cannot be hurt may be deeply afraid of the next blow. Perhaps you created a persona with no room for fear or weakness. Boundaries are important, but denying vulnerability is not the same as finding safety. Protection begins by recognizing that harm is possible.
225.history: Pac's Life included both a Swizz Beatz-produced version featuring Bone Thugs-n-Harmony and another version with Outlawz. Released in 2006, these arrangements use Tupac vocals recorded before his death, with new guest parts added later. The song projects street toughness and invulnerability.
225.details: 2Pac | Pac's Life | Two versions released November 21, 2006, posthumously

226.headline: Being famous is not the same as being understood.
226.fortune: Everyone may have an opinion about your life, but how many have actually seen it up close? Maybe people assembled a complete story about you from a few photos and headlines. You do not need to fight every false interpretation. Your life is bigger than other people's incomplete accounts. Knowing your name does not mean knowing you.
226.history: Featuring Ashanti and T.I., this track explores public curiosity and judgment surrounding Tupac's life. Released on Pac's Life in 2006, it also has a version with Snoop Dogg. Tupac's original part predates 1996, while later guest performances were added after his death.
226.details: 2Pac feat. Ashanti & T.I. | Pac's Life | Released November 21, 2006, posthumously

227.headline: Real loyalty sometimes means stopping the fight.
227.fortune: Some groups make you feel safe only because everyone is ready to fight. Maybe you think supporting a friend requires joining every conflict without thinking. Loyalty becomes dangerous when it takes away your judgment. A real friend does not simply stand beside the fire; sometimes they stop it from spreading.
227.history: Tupac, Hussein Fatal, and guests added for the 2006 version portray street groups, weapons, and violent confrontation. Released on Pac's Life using older Tupac recordings, the track's dominant tone is combative rather than conciliatory.
227.details: 2Pac feat. Hussein Fatal | Pac's Life | Released November 21, 2006, posthumously

228.headline: Hope is not a substitute for clear promises.
228.fortune: Every relationship can begin with a dream, but a dream does not replace honest commitments. Maybe you imagine a future with someone without discussing fears or responsibilities. Dreams matter, but knowing the actual person matters even more. Love grows deeper when reality is allowed to stand beside imagination.
228.history: Tupac addresses love, fear of prison or death, and hopes of having a family. Pac's Life (2006) includes a 'Female' version with Keyshia Cole and a 'Male' version with Ludacris. Because the main Tupac verse is shared, both versions count as one fortune.
228.details: 2Pac | Pac's Life | Female and Male versions released November 21, 2006

229.headline: The next step should be yours to choose.
229.fortune: When a crisis ends, the next question can be more frightening than the crisis itself: now what? Perhaps you spent years trying to clear one obstacle but never planned what to do afterward. You do not need the answer to your entire life. Sometimes the most important move is recognizing which next step is truly yours.
229.history: Released on Pac's Life in 2006, the track uses older Tupac vocals with new production. It deals with money, rivalry, dangerous choices, and an uncertain future in street life. Its question about what comes next is asked in a threatening atmosphere.

230.headline: You need more than staying awake to keep going.
230.fortune: If you stay on guard even when it is time to sleep, your body will eventually pay the price. Maybe relaxing has become difficult because you are always expecting something bad. Be careful when caution becomes a habit of living in fear. Surviving tomorrow requires more than never closing your eyes.
230.history: In 'Sleep,' Tupac describes sleeplessness and constant vigilance around weapons, money, and threats. A 2006 version with Young Buck and Chamillionaire appeared on Pac's Life. The lyrics depict danger and lost rest, but cannot establish a clinical diagnosis or a precise account of Tupac's sleep.
230.details: 2Pac feat. Young Buck & Chamillionaire | Pac's Life | Released November 21, 2006, posthumously

231.headline: Changing places does not automatically change your habits.
231.fortune: You may believe that traveling farther has made you a completely new person. But some habits follow you everywhere. A change of place creates an opportunity, not a guaranteed change of mind. Before building a new life, ask what you do not want to carry with you. Geographic distance is not distance from yourself.
231.history: Featuring Nipsey Hussle and Young Dre the Truth, the track appeared on Pac's Life in 2006 using older Tupac vocals. Despite the international title, much of the song addresses sexual relationships, bravado, and West Coast identity rather than documented travel across countries.
231.details: 2Pac feat. Nipsey Hussle & Young Dre the Truth | Pac's Life | Released November 21, 2006

232.headline: Stay alert without living in permanent alarm.
232.fortune: When you are always watching for an opportunity, you risk missing the experience of life itself. Maybe fear of falling behind leaves you unable to pause. Staying attentive is useful, but permanent emergency mode wears you down. Keep your eyes open without expecting the next blow every moment.
232.history: Tupac and later-added guests rap about readiness, street credibility, and threats. Released on Pac's Life in 2006, the arrangement includes Lil Scrappy and other performances added after Tupac's death. It is distinct from the song 'Sleep' and has different lyrical content.
232.details: 2Pac feat. Lil Scrappy | Pac's Life | Released November 21, 2006, posthumously

233.headline: Coming back should mean more than repeating the past.
233.fortune: Some people dream of leaving a confined place just to see someone again. Maybe you have promised to make things right later. If you get the chance to return, physical presence alone may not be enough; ask what the relationship needs to repair. A return matters when it changes something, not only when it repeats.
233.history: Tupac speaks in a letter-like voice from prison to someone close, mixing hopes of return with fear and distrust. Featuring Yaki Kadafi, it appeared on Pac's Life in 2006. It is among the album's few tracks whose original arrangement was preserved.
233.details: 2Pac feat. Yaki Kadafi | Pac's Life | Released November 21, 2006, posthumously

234.headline: You can speak freely and still take responsibility.
234.fortune: When someone threatens to silence a voice, asking 'why?' becomes important. Maybe your words make someone uncomfortable, and they would rather shut you down than answer. Freedom of speech matters, but so do the effects of our words. You do not have to choose between staying silent and speaking without thought.
234.history: In parts of 'Don't Stop,' Tupac responds to attacks on rap and freedom of expression, naming critics such as C. Delores Tucker. The 2006 Pac's Life album version combines his earlier vocal with Outlawz performances. The song relates to political disputes over violent rap content.
234.details: 2Pac feat. Outlawz | Pac's Life | Released November 21, 2006, posthumously

235.headline: Pain explains some choices; it does not excuse every choice.
235.fortune: A pain nobody sees is still real. Perhaps those around you judge only the results of your decisions without knowing the pressure behind them. Not everyone has to understand you, but you must not turn suffering into permission to hurt others. Pain can explain what happened without making every action right.
235.history: With Stretch, Tupac sings about life under pressure, betrayal, danger, and pain. Known from the film Above the Rim, the song appeared on the soundtrack cassette in 1994 but was absent from some early CD editions. It belongs to his pre-Death Row period.
235.details: 2Pac feat. Stretch | Above the Rim soundtrack | Cassette release 1994

236.headline: Something that numbs the pain may not address its cause.
236.fortune: Sometimes we escape our thoughts through something that quiets them for a little while. Maybe you have confused a short-lived habit with real peace. You do not need to shame yourself; simply notice how you feel afterward. A thing that silences pain is not necessarily a thing that heals it.
236.history: This track appeared on the 1996 Sunset Park soundtrack amid themes of substance use, street pressure, and hard-edged identity. Tupac recorded it with producer Tony Pizarro. Its title and lyrics should not be treated as a recommendation to use drugs; they are part of the street persona.

237.headline: Running without understanding the danger only changes the route.
237.fortune: When you constantly feel pursued, nowhere seems safe. Maybe your days have become a series of responses to real or imagined threats. To find a way out, ask which dangers truly follow you and which fears you carry along yourself. Escaping without understanding what frightens you may just lead to another detour.
237.history: Tupac and Snoop Doggy Dogg collaborated on this track for the 1997 Gridlock'd soundtrack, tied to a film starring Tupac. Produced by Daz Dillinger, it evokes being hunted and displaying street power. Their voices were recorded while Tupac was still alive.
237.details: 2Pac & Snoop Doggy Dogg | Gridlock'd soundtrack | Released January 1997, posthumously

238.headline: Sometimes courage means admitting today was hard.
238.fortune: Smiling does not always mean you feel okay. Maybe you keep hiding pain behind jokes so other people will not worry. You do not need to fall apart in front of everyone, but you deserve at least one safe person with whom you can be real. Sometimes courage is choosing honesty over a forced smile.
238.history: Released in 1997, 'Smile' features Scarface, Tupac, and Johnny P. It became one of Tupac's better-known collaborations heard by the public after his death. Its subject is enduring suffering, violence, and loss. Their shared recording predates his death.
238.details: Scarface feat. 2Pac & Johnny P | Released 1997, posthumously

239.headline: Thinking independently can be hardest in a crowd.
239.fortune: When a group makes you feel brave, it becomes harder to distinguish courage from danger. Maybe around friends you do things you would never choose alone. Loyalty need not mean accepting every conflict. Sometimes the most difficult act in a group is refusing to let others do your thinking.
239.history: Tupac's collaboration with Bone Thugs-n-Harmony appeared on their 1997 album The Art of War. Fast, tense music and gunshot-like effects accompany threatening lyrics and displays of street power. The album version reached listeners after Tupac's death.
239.details: Bone Thugs-n-Harmony feat. 2Pac | The Art of War | Released 1997, posthumously

240.headline: Belonging should never cost you your judgment.
240.fortune: Every group has unwritten tests for admission. Maybe you feel pressure to prove you are just like everyone else. Before accepting those invisible rules, ask whether you can still be yourself. Acceptance feels good, but not at any price. Joining a group should not mean switching off your judgment.
240.history: This track features Daz Dillinger, Tupac, Kurupt, and Outlawz and was released on the 1998 album Retaliation, Revenge and Get Back. It describes entry into a circle of street companions, displays of power, and readiness for conflict. Tupac's voice was recorded before his death.
240.details: Daz Dillinger feat. 2Pac, Kurupt & Outlawz | Retaliation, Revenge and Get Back | Released 1998, posthumously
